descriptionChirho: To actively bestow blessing or invoke divine favor upon someone (Piel stem); the primary and most frequent sense of barak, covering all Piel finite forms, imperatives, infinitives, participles, and consecutive forms where the subject blesses an object or God.
Adjectival state of being blessed, used predicatively or as an exclamation of praise (Qal passive participle barukh); Arabic mubarak, Korean bok-issda, conveying a state rather than an action.

Passive of the Piel, indicating the subject receives blessing; Arabic yubarak (passive voice), Korean bok-bat-da, distinct from the Qal participle by expressing an event of being blessed rather than a state.

Reflexive-reciprocal sense where nations or individuals bless themselves or count themselves blessed through association; Arabic tatab_raku (reflexive Form V/VI), indicating self-invoked or mediated blessing.
The original physical sense of the root: to bend the knee, kneel in worship or submission; Arabic nabruka (let us kneel), raka'a (he knelt), Korean mureup-kkulda.
Causative of the Qal physical sense: to make someone or something kneel down; Arabic anakha (he made kneel), used of making camels kneel.

Euphemistic use of barak in Piel meaning 'to curse' or 'to blaspheme', a well-known scribal substitution to avoid writing the direct word for cursing God; Arabic jaddafa (blaspheme), Swahili laani (curse), Korean jeoju-hada.
